author: Bowling, Lawrence E.
title: What Is the Stream of Consciousness Technique?
relevance: Foundational statement of SoC as a *technique*; the locus classicus of the technique-side position the framework's 'technique evidence' pole descends from.

author: Humphrey, Robert
title: Stream of Consciousness in the Modern Novel
relevance: The four-type typology the whole framework tests; source of the 'technique evidence' categories.

author: Friedman, Melvin J.
title: Stream of Consciousness: A Study in Literary Method
relevance: Companion foundational study treating SoC as literary method; reinforces the technique/method framing.

author: Dahl, Liisa
title: Linguistic Features of the Stream-of-Consciousness Techniques of Woolf, Joyce and O'Neill
relevance: Early linguistic operationalization of SoC markers — a precedent for the framework's feature-based classification.

author: Cohn, Dorrit
title: Transparent Minds: Narrative Modes for Presenting Consciousness in Fiction
relevance: Refines Humphrey's coarse types into psycho-narration / quoted monologue / narrated monologue — directly reframes the 'boundary tension' pole and the omniscient-description category.

author: Genette, Gérard
title: Narrative Discourse: An Essay in Method
relevance: Systematizes mood/voice distinctions underlying any typological sort of narration; background for boundary-tension rigor.

author: Banfield, Ann
title: Unspeakable Sentences: Narration and Representation in the Language of Fiction
relevance: Linguistic theory of represented speech/thought; the strong claim that FID is a distinct grammatical form bears on whether 'boundary tension' is real or artefactual.

author: McHale, Brian
title: Unspeakable Sentences, Unnatural Acts: Linguistics and Poetics Revisited
relevance: Influential critique of Banfield; models exactly the kind of boundary-drawing debate the framework calls 'boundary tension.'

author: Fludernik, Monika
title: The Fictions of Language and the Languages of Fiction
relevance: Comprehensive account of FID/represented consciousness that dissolves rigid type boundaries into a cline — evidence the technique/genre binary is graded.

author: Fludernik, Monika
title: Towards a 'Natural' Narratology
relevance: Grounds narrative in cognitive 'natural' frames rather than fixed forms; a theoretical basis for treating SoC as experientiality rather than a closed typology.

author: Palmer, Alan
title: The Construction of Fictional Minds
relevance: Programmatic statement of the fictional-minds turn; reframes the technique pole as one means among many of building a mind, weakening a purely form-based taxonomy.

author: Palmer, Alan
title: Fictional Minds
relevance: Book-length cognitive account of consciousness in fiction; the major challenge to a technique-first classification.

author: Zunshine, Lisa
title: Why We Read Fiction: Theory of Mind and the Novel
relevance: Theory-of-mind account of reading consciousness; supports reader-convergence as evidence (the framework's multi-reader criterion).

author: Herman, David
title: The Emergence of Mind: Representations of Consciousness in Narrative Discourse in English
relevance: Historicizes consciousness-representation techniques across periods; situates Humphrey's types as one historical stratum, not a universal grid.

author: Caracciolo, Marco
title: Punctuating Minds: Non-verbal Cues for Consciousness Representation in Literary Interpretation
relevance: Treats typographic/orthographic cues (the framework's device #7) as cognitive prompts — bridges technique markers and reader experience.

author: Richardson, Brian
title: Unnatural Voices: Extreme Narration in Modern and Contemporary Fiction
relevance: Theorizes narration that exceeds mimetic/typological categories — the closest existing theory of the framework's 'genre evidence' (no-type-fits) pole.

author: Alber, Jan
title: Unnatural Narratives, Unnatural Narratology: Beyond Mimetic Models
relevance: Core statement of the unnatural program; theorizes reading strategies for passages that resist naturalized (typological) frames — the genre pole.

author: Alber, Jan
title: What Is Unnatural about Unnatural Narratology?: A Response to Monika Fludernik
relevance: Defines 'unnatural' as antimimetic and non-conventionalized — sharpens the criterion for 'no single type fits.'

author: Fludernik, Monika
title: How Natural Is 'Unnatural Narratology'; or, What Is Unnatural about Unnatural Narratology?
relevance: The counter-position: 'unnatural' features get conventionalized over time — a caution that today's genre-evidence may be tomorrow's technique.

author: Bowler, Rebecca; Drewery, Claire
title: One Hundred Years of the Stream of Consciousness: Editors' Introduction
relevance: Already cited by the framework; the current-state overview arguing the definition is 'fraught with contradictions' — the anchor for the genre-side skepticism.

author: Guy, Adam
title: Who Cares about the Stream of Consciousness? On Dorothy Richardson's Pilgrimage and the Time of Reading
relevance: Directly interrogates whether SoC is a coherent object; centres Richardson (the framework's puzzle author) and the reading-time dimension.

author: Long, Hoyt; So, Richard Jean
title: Literary Pattern Recognition: Modernism between Close Reading and Machine Learning
relevance: The framework already cites this; the flagship demonstration that SoC/haiku-style form can be learned computationally — precedent and benchmark for the fit-score method.

author: Underwood, Ted
title: The Life Cycles of Genres
relevance: Empirical modelling of genre as a diachronic, fuzzy category — a computational model for treating 'genre evidence' as gradient rather than binary.

author: Da, Nan Z.
title: The Computational Case against Computational Literary Studies
relevance: The major methodological critique of CLS; the essential caution for the fit-ratio/classifier program — statistical patterns can be brittle or uninterpretable.

author: Underwood, Ted
title: Distant Horizons: Digital Evidence and Literary Change
relevance: Argues distant methods capture gradient literary change; supports per-work 'fit ratios' as legitimate evidence when validated.

author: Gast, Volker
title: A Register-Based Study of Interior Monologue in James Joyce's Ulysses
relevance: Recent corpus/register operationalization of interior monologue in the framework's central text — a direct methodological sibling and comparison point.
